issues.legal_issue: A preliminary vacancy order may be challenged in a statutory revision against the final allotment order even if it was not successfully challenged separately when made.
material_facts: The occupants challenged the vacancy order in an earlier writ proceeding, which was dismissed subject to express liberty to challenge the vacancy order after the final order.
After the final order was made, the occupants challenged both that order and the vacancy order in a statutory revision.
The revisional court set aside the vacancy and final orders, but the High Court held that the vacancy order could not be challenged in that revision.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in holding that the revision was not maintainable on the ground that the vacancy order could not be challenged along with the final order.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 18 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, a vacancy order is a preliminary step leading to the final allotment order and may be challenged in a revision against that final order, absent a statutory provision precluding that challenge or making the vacancy order final. Achal Misra v. Rama Shanker Singh held that an aggrieved person may challenge the vacancy order immediately by writ petition or challenge it with the final order in the statutory proceeding. Ganpat Roy v. ADM did not hold that failure to challenge immediately forfeits the later challenge; Tirlok Singh was disapproved to the extent inconsistent with that rule. The principle is consistent with Section 105(1) and Order 43 Rule 1-A of the Code of Civil Procedure and the decisions in Moheshur Sing v. Bengal Govt., Sheonoth v. Ramnath, and Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi, subject to the exceptions in Sections 97 and 105(2) of that Code.

rule.if: rent_control_allotment_proceeding and vacancy_order_is_preliminary and final_allotment_order_made and revision_challenges_final_order and not statutory_bar_to_later_challenge

predicates.rent_control_allotment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the control of a rented building and its allotment after a vacancy determination.
predicates.vacancy_order_is_preliminary: The vacancy determination is a step in the process leading to a final allotment or release order.
predicates.final_allotment_order_made: The authority has made the final order that follows the vacancy determination.
predicates.revision_challenges_final_order: An aggrieved person seeks statutory revision of the final order and also challenges the preliminary vacancy determination.
predicates.statutory_bar_to_later_challenge: A law expressly precludes a later challenge to the preliminary order or gives that order final effect.
predicates.vacancy_order_challenge_permissible: The preliminary vacancy determination may be challenged in the statutory revision against the final order.

issues.definition: When a vacancy determination is preliminary, a final order has been made, and the revision challenges that final order, the preliminary determination may also be challenged unless a statutory bar applies.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant is not deemed to have vacated a rented building merely because other people reside there alongside the tenant or the tenant’s family; the relevant occupation must be by a non-family member in that person’s own right.
material_facts: The inspection report recorded that the original tenant’s son and family, the tenant’s brother’s family, and other relatives were residing in the premises.
The report did not establish that a person outside the tenant’s family had been given possession to occupy the premises in that person’s own right.
The vacancy finding treated the presence of the other occupants as sufficient to establish deemed vacancy.
issues.conclusion: The premises were not deemed vacant on the facts recorded in the inspection report, and the vacancy finding was contrary to the governing interpretation of the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(1)(b) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 applies where the tenant has allowed a person who is not a member of the tenant’s family to occupy the building in that person’s own right. In Harish Tandon v. Addl. District Magistrate, Allahabad, the Court held that mere residence by another person alongside the tenant or the tenant’s family does not satisfy that requirement; the significant words are “allowed” and “occupy.”

predicates.rent_control_vacancy_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a rented building is vacant because of the occupants’ use of it.
predicates.tenant_or_tenant_family_resides_in_premi: The tenant or members of the tenant’s family reside in the premises.
predicates.other_occupants_reside_alongside_tenant_: Other people reside in the premises alongside the tenant or the tenant’s family.
predicates.no_nonfamily_occupies_in_own_right: No person outside the tenant’s family has been given possession to occupy the premises in that person’s own right.
predicates.premises_not_deemed_vacant: The presence of the other occupants does not make the premises deemed vacant.

issues.definition: Where the tenant or the tenant’s family resides with other occupants and no non-family occupant possesses the premises in that person’s own right, the premises are not deemed vacant.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory revisional authority may correct a finding that rests on an error of law or a material defect in the treatment of evidence, but may not interfere merely because it would reach a different factual view.
material_facts: The rent authority declared the premises vacant despite the inspection report recording that the occupants were the tenant’s relatives and were residing alongside the tenant’s family.
The rent authority’s finding was contrary to the legal test for deemed vacancy and rested on a misreading or disregard of the inspection evidence.
The District Judge set aside the vacancy and final orders in statutory revision.
issues.conclusion: The District Judge was justified in interfering because the rent authority’s order applied the law incorrectly and was based on a misreading or ignorance of the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18(1) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 permits revision on grounds including exercise of jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity. Revisional jurisdiction is narrower than appellate jurisdiction: it does not permit reappraisal merely to substitute a different factual view, but does permit correction of findings contrary to law, based on misread or omitted material evidence, unsupported by evidence, or otherwise perverse. The Court applied Sarla Ahuja v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Ram Narain Arora v. Asha Rani, Harshavardhan Chokkani v. Bhupendra N. Patel, and the Constitution Bench decision in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Dilbahar Singh.

predicates.rent_control_statutory_revision: A party seeks review under a statute that gives a revisional authority limited power over a rent authority’s order.
predicates.challenged_order_has_material_legality_d: The challenged order violates governing law, misreads or omits material evidence, rests on no evidence, or contains a comparably serious error in its findings.
predicates.revisional_interference_permissible: The revisional authority may correct the challenged order.

issues.definition: In a statutory rent-control revision, a material legal or evidentiary defect in the challenged order permits revisional correction.

issues.legal_issue: Supervisory jurisdiction cannot be used to convert the reviewing court into an appellate court or to correct mere errors where the subordinate tribunal has acted within its authority.
material_facts: The District Judge exercised statutory revisional jurisdiction and set aside the rent authority’s orders for legal error and misreading of the evidence.

The High Court reversed the District Judge on the mistaken view that the vacancy order could not be challenged in the revision, while disregarding the governing precedent and the express liberty reserved in the earlier proceeding.
The District Judge’s decision was within the scope of the statutory revisional power.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s exercise of supervisory jurisdiction was unwarranted and unjustified, and its order was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 of the Constitution of India gives the High Court supervisory power to keep subordinate courts and tribunals within the bounds of their authority and ensure that they obey the law; it does not confer appellate power to correct mere errors. The Court relied on Satyanarayan Laxminarayan Hegde v. Millikarjun Bhavanappa Tirumale, Bathutmal Raichand Oswal v. Laxmibai R. Tarta, India Pipe Fitting Co. v. Fakruddin M. A. Baker, Ganpat Ladha v. Sashikant Vishnu Shinde, Labhkuwar Bhagwani Shaha v. Janardhan Mahadeo Kalan, Chandavarkar Sita Ratna Rao v. Ashalata S. Guram, Venkatlal G. Pittie v. Bright Bros. (P) Ltd., State of Maharashtra v. Milind, State v. Navjot Sandhu, Ranjeet Singh v. Ravi Prakash, Shamshad Ahmad v. Tilak Raj Bajaj, and Celina Coelho Pereira v. Ulhas Mahabaleshwar Kholkar.

predicates.supervisory_review_of_subordinate_tribun: A higher court is exercising supervisory review over a subordinate court or tribunal.
predicates.subordinate_tribunal_within_authority: The subordinate tribunal acted within the limits of its authority.
predicates.no_serious_jurisdictional_or_legality_er: The subordinate tribunal’s decision does not contain a serious jurisdictional or legal defect requiring supervisory correction.
predicates.supervisory_court_corrects_only_mere_err: The reviewing court intervenes only to correct an error rather than to remedy a serious defect or keep the tribunal within its authority.
predicates.supervisory_interference_unwarranted: The higher court’s intervention exceeds the proper scope of supervisory jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When a tribunal acts within its authority without a serious jurisdictional or legal defect, supervisory intervention solely to correct an error is unwarranted.
